prize_parts.citation: for the theory of credit cycles, showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate economic shocks

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identify a specific and portable mechanism. Credit limits tied to the value of collateral assets create a feedback loop between asset prices and borrowing capacity, so small or temporary shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. The idea is a general building block of macro-finance and is used in models of crises and macroprudential policy. Attribution is clean: the originating paper is jointly theirs, and a two-name prize needs no hard exclusions. The work is about three decades old, so it has been extended and used extensively, especially since 2008. The 2022 prize covered banks, bank runs and the empirical study of financial crises, not the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism, so I see it as a distinct discovery. The committee can state the discovery in a single sentence, which is not true of the more diffuse candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic proximity to the 2022 prize (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig). Several colleagues see this as lowering the marginal priority of financial-friction macro. A second concern is that the evidence base is largely one theoretical paper and the literature it spawned. Direct empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is still debated, and the quantitative fit of these models is imperfect. Third, excluding Gertler and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator line is a judgement that some will contest. If the committee weights breadth of confirmed empirical use and trade's absence from the prize since 2008, B012 is at least as defensible and I would support it.

responses.point: Boppart ranks Kiyotaki-Moore fifth and proposes a two-person award. He notes that related financial-crisis work was recognised in 2022, which may reduce its marginal priority, and he asks whether Gertler should join.
responses.response: I agree that two names is the defensible size, and I keep Gertler out for the same reason. I only partly agree on 2022. The Diamond-Dybvig and Bernanke contributions concern bank runs, intermediation and the empirical anatomy of the Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore is a real-side amplification mechanism that works through the price of a durable collateral asset, without needing a bank or a run. That difference is real, but it is a judgement the committee should make explicitly. I treat it as a risk to the case rather than a settled point. I also share Boppart's view that B012 is a very strong competitor, and I rank it second.

responses.point: Teorell sees Kiyotaki-Moore and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator as two pillars. He thinks Bernanke's absence from the credited list and his earlier prize make a clean three-person attribution awkward, and he notes that Gertler also appears on the New Keynesian ballot.
responses.response: I read the same problem as an argument for the narrower prize. The accelerator works through agency costs and an external finance premium. The collateral-constraint mechanism is a different channel, and one paper clearly originated it. Adding Gertler would mean either splitting the citation across two mechanisms or counting his work on B021 twice. A two-name prize avoids both. The cost is that the accelerator strand stays unrecognised. I accept that cost, and I would revisit it only if the committee wants one broad financial-frictions citation, which I think is harder to justify on attribution.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B029 first. He argues that the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand-estimation framework is cleanly attributable, has proven practical impact in merger and antitrust work, and has no timing problem, though he worries about a methods prize so soon after 2021.
responses.response: I largely agree on the merits and rank B029 third. Attribution to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn is as clean as it gets on a seven-name list. Where I differ is on what each prize rewards. In my reading, B043 rewards a conceptual mechanism about how economies behave. B029 rewards an estimation toolkit, so it faces the committee's question about whether a methods prize is wanted soon after 2021. I am not sure that gives B043 an edge. Bresnahan's claim is the real unresolved point in B029, and I would want that settled before supporting it ahead of a clean two-name alternative.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 first with a two-person award. He treats Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions as derivative of Melitz's core insight, and he raises Bernard, Jensen and Eaton-Kortum as possible co-claimants.
responses.response: I agree on limiting B012 to Melitz and Helpman, and I rank it second for the same reasons. Redding's work is substantial but extends the framework rather than originating it. The parallel Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum contributions are an attribution risk on any trade candidate, and the three-name cap cannot resolve them. They are one reason I put B043 slightly ahead, because its attribution risk is smaller. That is a narrow margin. I do not claim my ordering is scientifically decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the collateral-constraint mechanism as distinct enough from the 2022 recognition of banks and financial crises.
Whether the committee prefers to add Gertler, which would bring in the financial-accelerator strand and entangle credit with Bernanke's earlier prize and with the Gertler names on B021.
How much weight direct empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification deserves when the case rests mainly on one theoretical paper and its follow-on literature.
Whether B012 or B029 offers a cleaner and more widely shared case than B043. My ordering of these three is close and rests on judgement.
My recollection of the credit shares across all candidates comes from general knowledge and is not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: I co-authored a 2026 paper (IJIO) with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. I disclose this and do not claim it bears on any shortlisted candidate. I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a public fact noted in my profile. No connection to any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from the supplied profile. My research fields (industrial organisation, trade and pricing) are adjacent to B012 and B029, and I treat that as expertise rather than merit.
